title: When AI starts acting on the user's behalf, UX needs to design limits
description: When AI carries out tasks, the user needs to understand what it will do, follow what it did and be able to stop or correct it.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: flows where AI agents, automations and human review work with visible limits and states.

blocks.text: The most important shift in an AI experience doesn't always happen when the answer gets more natural. It happens when the system stops just answering and starts carrying out tasks.
An AI that suggests options works one way. An agent that searches, compares, fills out forms or starts a purchase calls for a different kind of experience.
The design question is no longer just “is the answer good?” It now includes: does the user understand what the system is going to do, what it has already done, and how to stop or correct the action?
Answering and acting are different experiences
In a traditional interface, the person picks an action and the system responds. In an agent experience, the person can state a goal while the system decides which steps to take.
That can cut repetitive work, but it also raises questions:

items: What information is the agent using?
Can it make a decision without asking for confirmation?
What happens if it misreads the goal?
How do I review what was done?
How do I cancel an action or go back?
Who is accountable when something goes wrong?

blocks.text: If the interface doesn't answer these questions, automation can feel convenient at first and unpredictable when something important happens.
Design levels of autonomy
A practical way to design the experience is to split actions into levels:
The agent presents a recommendation, but the person decides.
The agent fills in fields or puts together a proposal, but waits for review.
The agent explains the action and asks for permission before doing it.
The person sets limits in advance, along with when the system needs to ask for confirmation.

This model is a design tool, not a universal standard. The right level depends on impact, reversibility and risk. Sorting a list is different from transferring money, canceling a service or sending a message on someone's behalf.
Confirmation needs to happen at the right moment
Asking for confirmation at every small step makes the experience exhausting. Not asking for confirmation on irreversible actions can create risks.
Consider three factors:

items: Impact: what's the consequence if the action is wrong?
Reversibility: is it easy to undo?
Ambiguity: are the goal and the required data clear?

blocks.text: The higher the impact and the lower the reversibility, the more important it is to explain the action and get explicit confirmation. For low-risk, reversible actions, it can make sense to allow automatic execution, as long as the person can follow what happened.
Show the task's state

A vague message like “working...” doesn't help when the agent runs several steps. When it's useful and safe, show understandable steps: finding options, comparing criteria, preparing a recommendation, waiting for confirmation and completing the action.
The interface needs to distinguish a completed step, a hypothesis, a pending action and an error. Don't present a task as done if the agent only prepared a suggestion.
Design for failure and recovery
The agent may misread an instruction, run into incomplete data or only partially complete an action. Good practices include:

items: Separating what was completed from what's still pending
Offering a clear way to try again
Letting people edit the data before retrying
Avoiding running an already completed action twice
Keeping a summary of the actions taken
Offering cancellation or rollback when possible.

blocks.text: The error experience is part of the product, not a detail to sort out after launch.
Checklist before launch

Test with users whether they understand which actions the agent can take, when there will be confirmation, how to review information, how to stop the process and how to recover from an error. Include scenarios with ambiguous instructions, dropped connections, partial results and actions outside the defined limits.
The quality of an agent experience doesn't depend only on how many tasks it automates. It depends on whether the person can delegate without losing understanding of and control over what matters.
